entries.description: The text the query was made with, read back. Read-only: the text is parsed once, in the constructor, and a query with another text is a new query — `New Query(StrReplace(Q.Text, ...))`. A query made without a text answers an empty string.
entries.example:
Q = New Query("SELECT G.Description AS Name FROM Catalog.Goods AS G");
Q2 = New Query(StrReplace(Q.Text, "Catalog.Goods", "Catalog.Services"));

entries.description: Gives the `&name` parameter of the text its value. The name is written without the ampersand. Setting it again replaces the value, so one query runs many times with different values without being parsed again. The value reaches the database as a bound parameter, never as part of the text. A parameter the text uses and nobody set is an execution error; a name the text does not use is kept and does nothing.
entries.parameters:
name — the parameter's name, without `&`.
value — a number, string, date, boolean, reference, PointInTime or Boundary; an Array or another collection for `IN (&name)`; a value table for `FROM &name`.
entries.example:
Q = New Query("SELECT COUNT(*) AS N FROM AccumulationRegister.Lots AS L WHERE L.Quantity > &Limit");
Q.SetParameter("Limit", 50);

entries.description:
Runs the query and answers with its result. Every call reads the data again. A text of several statements runs whole, as a package, and Execute answers with the FIRST statement's result — for an ordinary query, the only one; the others are read with ExecuteBatch.

A query with no text, or whose first statement is a DROP, answers an empty result: its Select walks nothing, and its Unload raises as if it had been read already. A statement that fails raises with that statement's message, and nothing after it runs; so does a parameter the text uses and nobody set.
entries.example:
Q = New Query("SELECT G.Description AS Name, G.Price AS Price FROM Catalog.Goods AS G");
Table = Q.Execute().Unload();

entries.description: Runs every statement of the text, in order, and answers with an Array of their results, by the position each statement was written at. A plain SELECT gives its QueryResult; a SELECT ... INTO a temporary table gives a result of one row and one column, the number of records it put there; a DROP gives Undefined. The statements see each other's temporary tables and one state of the data.
entries.return_descr: Array — a QueryResult or Undefined per statement.

entries.description:
Where this query's temporary tables live. Left unset, the tables a text makes with INTO die with the execution that made them. Set to a TempTablesManager, they outlive it: another query given the same manager reads them by name, until the manager is closed.

Anything other than a TempTablesManager raises at once; Undefined clears it, and the query goes back to keeping its tables for one run.

A home for temporary tables that must outlive one execution. Give the same manager to several queries (their TempTablesManager property): what one query puts INTO a temporary table, the next reads by the table's name. Close releases them; so does the manager going away.

Without a manager a package still shares its temporary tables between its own statements — a manager is needed only when the tables must cross from one Query to another.
Drops every temporary table the manager holds. A query that reads one of them afterwards fails: the name no longer stands for a table.

entries.signature: Select(iteration : QueryResultIteration = Direct, branch : string = "") : QuerySelect
entries.description:
Opens a walk over the result's rows. Direct (the default) reads the rows as they are; ByGroups walks a TOTALS result level by level, a group node first and its rows under it; ByGroupsHierarchy also unfolds a dimension along its hierarchy.

`branch` walks one branch of a SPLIT totals result from the top; a name no branch answers to gives an empty walk. Left out, every branch, in order.

A result is read once: Select takes its rows, and a second Select answers an empty walk — run the query again.
entries.parameters:
iteration — a QueryResultIteration value; left out, Direct.
branch — the name of a SPLIT branch; left out, all of them.

entries.description:
The result's rows as a value table: one column per output column, named and typed as the query names and types it. For a script that counts, indexes, sorts or hands the rows on rather than walking them once.

It reads the result, as Select does: a second Unload raises ("already been read") rather than answering an empty table that would look like "found nothing". Only the Direct iteration unloads — a grouped result is a tree and is walked with Select; asking for ByGroups raises before anything is read.
entries.example:
Table = New Query("SELECT G.Description AS Name, G.Price AS Price FROM Catalog.Goods AS G").Execute().Unload();
Message(String(Table.Count()) + " goods, " + String(Table.Total("Price")) + " in all");

entries.description: How a query result is walked: QueryResult.Select and QuerySelect.Select take a member, written QueryResultIteration.<Name>. Direct reads the rows as they are; the other two walk a TOTALS result as a tree.
The rows as they are, one after another, at one level. The default; the only iteration Unload takes.
A TOTALS result level by level: the selection hands out the group nodes of the first BY dimension, and each node's Select descends to the next level. An aggregated column reads the node's subtotal.
As ByGroups, and a reference dimension totalled BY ... HIERARCHY is unfolded along its catalog's folders: a folder is a node, its elements and subfolders are under it.
Moves to the next row — the first one on the first call — and answers True, or False when there are no more. A row's columns are read only after Next has answered True.

Puts a GROUPED selection (ByGroups, ByGroupsHierarchy, or any walk of a TOTALS result) back before its first node, to walk it again. A flat selection is a forward cursor and cannot go back: Reset leaves it where it is — run the query again, or Unload the rows into a table and walk that as often as needed.
The depth of the current node in a TOTALS tree: 0 for the grand total and for every row of a flat selection, one more for each BY dimension below it.
Whether the current node of a TOTALS tree has nodes or rows under it, which its Select would hand out. Always False on a flat selection.

entries.signature: Select(iteration : QueryResultIteration = Direct, branch : string = "") : QuerySelect
entries.description:
Descends into the current node of a TOTALS tree: a new selection over the nodes and rows under it, walked with its own Next. `iteration` says how that level is walked, as for QueryResult.Select; `branch` takes one branch where the totals split (SPLIT) — left out, every branch in order.

On a flat selection there is nothing under a row, and the answer is an empty selection.
entries.parameters:
iteration — a QueryResultIteration value; left out, Direct.
branch — a SPLIT branch's name; left out, all of them.

entries.description: The grand total of an aggregated column over the whole TOTALS result, whichever node the selection stands on. The column is named as the query names it, regardless of case. A flat selection has no totals and answers Undefined; so does a name the query does not have — check the spelling when a total comes back empty.
entries.parameters: column — the output column's name (the attribute name or its AS alias).

entries.signature: New Boundary(position : Date | PointInTime, kind : BoundaryKind = Including)
entries.description:
A position, and which side of it is meant. The position is what a register reading already takes — a date, or a PointInTime naming a document at its date; the kind says whether the row standing exactly at that position is inside (Including) or outside (Excluding).

It is what makes "the balance BEFORE this document" sayable: `Boundary(Document.PointInTime(), BoundaryKind.Excluding)` stops just before the document, whatever else was written at the same second. A bare date or PointInTime means Including.

Taken wherever a register reading takes its period — a balance, a turnover period, a slice, a virtual table's parameter — and by Sequence.Restore.
entries.parameters:
position — a date or a PointInTime.
kind — BoundaryKind.Including (the default) or BoundaryKind.Excluding.
entries.example:
Q = New Query("SELECT B.Item AS Item, B.QuantityBalance AS Qty FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&Period) AS B");
Q.SetParameter("Period", New Boundary(Doc.PointInTime(), BoundaryKind.Excluding));   // the balance before Doc

entries.description: The position the boundary stands at — the first argument of New Boundary. Read and written.

Whether the position itself is inside the interval. Written with a BoundaryKind value. Read back, it answers the member's NUMBER — 0 for Including, 1 for Excluding — not the BoundaryKind value, so compare it with a number: `Bound.Kind = 1`.
Whether a Boundary's own position belongs to the interval it bounds. Written BoundaryKind.<Name>; New Boundary takes it as its second argument, and Boundary.Kind is set with it.
The position is inside: a reading up to it takes the row standing exactly there. What a bare date or PointInTime has always meant; the default.
The position is outside: a reading up to it stops just before the row standing there — the balance before a document, not after it.

A date and, optionally, the document that sits at it. A date alone cannot tell apart two documents written in the same second; the pair can, and "everything up to THIS document" is the question register readings are asked.

Moments are ordered by the date first and the reference second, and a moment with no reference stands BEFORE every moment of the same date that has one — it is the instant itself, before anything recorded in it. Compared with a plain Date (`<`, `>`, Compare) the date alone decides; but `=` is strict: a PointInTime never equals a Date.

Built by hand rarely: a document (and other objects that stand at a moment) answers its own with `PointInTime()`. Register readings, query parameters and a Boundary take it wherever they take a date.
entries.syntax_block:
Moment = New PointInTime(Date, Reference);
Moment = Doc.PointInTime();
entries.parameters:
date — a Date; anything else is refused.
reference — the document at that date; left out or Undefined, the instant itself.
entries.example:
Q = New Query("SELECT B.Item AS Item, B.QuantityBalance AS Qty FROM AccumulationRegister.Stock.Balance(&Period) AS B");
Q.SetParameter("Period", Doc.PointInTime());   // the balance after Doc, not after its whole second

entries.description: The moment's date. Read and written. An empty date makes the moment empty.
The document at the moment's date, or Undefined when the moment is the instant itself. Read and written.

-1 when this moment is earlier than `other`, 1 when later, 0 when they stand at the same place — the same order `<` and `>` use, in one call. Against a plain Date only the date is compared, so a moment of that date compares 0 with it.
entries.parameters: other — a PointInTime or a Date.

entries.description:
A data source as a value: a catalog, a document, a register, a constant — the same source the query language reads with FROM — or an in-memory value table given to `Data.From(table)`. Never made with New: `Data.Catalogs.Goods`, `Data.AccumulationRegisters.Lots`.

It is read with the LINQ verbs, and they BUILD A QUERY rather than read rows. Where, Select, OrderBy, OrderByDescending and Take fold into it and answer a new Queryable; Count, Any, First, FirstOrDefault, ToArray and ToTable run it on the server; Join runs on the server when both sides allow it. Holding a Queryable reads nothing — a watch shows what it would read, `Queryable(AccumulationRegisters.Lots | Where, Take 5)`.

Any other verb (GroupBy, Skip, Distinct, Sum, Union...) and a lambda that does not translate run IN MEMORY: what has been folded so far is read, every row of it, and the verb runs over those rows, answering a LINQ sequence (LinqQuery) rather than a Queryable. The rows are the same, the cost is not — the technology journal says which step fell to memory and why.

A catalog's, document's or chart's rows come as references; a register's, a constant's and a value table's as Structures of their columns. Foreach streams them row by row.
entries.syntax_block:
Rows = Data.Catalogs.Goods
    .Where(Function(g) { return g.Price > 100; })
    .OrderBy(Function(g) { return g.Description; })
    .Take(20)
    .ToArray();
entries.syntax_block_ves:
Rows = Data.Catalogs.Goods
    .Where(Function(g) Return g.Price > 100; EndFunction)
    .OrderBy(Function(g) Return g.Description; EndFunction)
    .Take(20)
    .ToArray();
entries.example:
Big = Data.AccumulationRegisters.Lots.Where(Function(x) { return x.Quantity > Limit; });
Message(String(Big.Count()) + " lots over " + String(Limit));

entries.description:
Narrows the source to the rows the predicate holds for, and answers a new Queryable; nothing is read yet. The lambda is translated into the query's WHERE: comparisons, AND / OR / NOT, a walk through a reference (`x.Item.Producer = P`), and the variables around it, read by name when it is folded.

A predicate that does not translate is not refused: the rows folded so far are read and filtered in memory, and the answer is a LINQ sequence rather than a Queryable: the verbs after it run in memory too. Without a function argument it raises.
entries.parameters: predicate — a function of one row that answers a boolean.
entries.return_descr: Queryable; when it ran in memory, a LINQ sequence (LinqQuery) — Foreach, Count and ToArray read it.
entries.example: Mine = Data.Documents.Sale.Where(Function(d) { return d.Counterparty = Client And d.Posted; });

entries.description:
Reads one value per row instead of the row: a column (`x => x.Price`), a walk through a reference (`x.Item.Description`), or arithmetic / a conditional over columns (`x.Price * x.Quantity`) — each becomes one output column of the query. Answers a new Queryable whose rows ARE those values.

A projection into a Structure (`{ A = x.A, B = x.B }`), or a second Select over the first, runs in memory over the rows read so far.
entries.parameters: projection — a function of one row.
entries.return_descr: Queryable; when it ran in memory, a LINQ sequence (LinqQuery) — Foreach, Count and ToArray read it.

entries.description: Orders the rows by a column of the source, ascending — or by a walk through a reference to one. The order becomes the query's ORDER BY. A key that is not a column (a computed value) runs in memory.
entries.parameters: key — a function of one row that names the column.
entries.return_descr: Queryable; when it ran in memory, a LINQ sequence (LinqQuery) — Foreach, Count and ToArray read it.

entries.description: As OrderBy, largest first.
entries.parameters: key — a function of one row that names the column.
entries.return_descr: Queryable; when it ran in memory, a LINQ sequence (LinqQuery) — Foreach, Count and ToArray read it.

entries.description: At most `count` rows: the query's row limit. Taken twice, the smaller limit stands. The count must be positive — 0 or less raises.

entries.signature: Join(inner : Queryable | Table, leftKey : Function, rightKey : Function, result : Function) : Array
entries.description:
Pairs each row with the rows of `inner` whose key equals its key, and answers what `result` makes of each pair `(row, innerRow)`. The join itself runs on the server when it can: `inner` is another source taken as it is (no Where or Take of its own) or a value table, each key is one column, and this side carries no OrderBy or Take. `result` always runs in memory over the joined rows.

Anything else — a computed key, a folded inner, a join of a source with itself — is joined in memory, with the same pairs. The answer is then a LINQ sequence rather than an Array: Foreach and Count read it, but it is not indexed — add `.ToArray()` to read `[i]`, which works on both.
entries.syntax_block:
Pairs = Outer.Join(Inner, Function(o) { return o.<Key>; }, Function(i) { return i.<Key>; },
    Function(o, i) { return New Structure("A, B", o.A, i.B); });
entries.parameters:
inner — a Queryable or a value Table.
leftKey — a function of this side's row naming its key column.
rightKey — a function of the inner row naming its key column.
result — a function of the pair that makes one element of the answer.
entries.return_descr: Array (joined on the server) or a LINQ sequence (joined in memory).

entries.description: How many rows the source holds after its Where — counted by the server (COUNT), no rows travel. A Take caps the answer.
Whether at least one row is there: the server is asked for one row, not for a count.
The first row, in the order folded so far — the server is asked for one row. On a source with no rows it answers Undefined: here First does not raise, it behaves as FirstOrDefault.
entries.return_descr: A row (a reference or a Structure), or Undefined.

entries.description: The first row, or Undefined when there is none. On a Queryable the same answer as First.
entries.return_descr: A row (a reference or a Structure), or Undefined.

entries.description: Runs the query and answers its rows as an Array: references for a catalog, document or chart; Structures of the columns for a register, a constant or a value table; the values themselves after a Select.
Runs the query and answers a value table with every column of the source, typed as the source types it — a table a form can show and `Data.From` can read again.

The data sources of one kind, by name: what `Data.Catalogs`, `Data.Documents`, `Data.InformationRegisters`, `Data.AccumulationRegisters`, `Data.AccountingRegisters`, `Data.CalculationRegisters`, `Data.Constants`, `Data.Enumerations`, `Data.ChartsOfAccounts`, `Data.ChartsOfCharacteristicTypes`, `Data.ChartsOfCalculationTypes` and `Data.Sequences` answer. Each source is read as a property by its name (`Data.Catalogs.Goods`) or with `["Goods"]`, and is a Queryable. Read-only; Foreach hands out the Queryables. Getting one reads no data.
How many sources of this kind the configuration has.
One source — by its position from 0, or by its name regardless of case. A name the kind does not have raises.
entries.parameters: index — the position, from 0; or name — the source's name.

entries.description: Folds a condition into the query being restricted — the very query that is running, not a copy. The lambda is translated against the restricted source's columns; a walk through a reference (`x.Contract.Company = C`) is answered as a correlated EXISTS, so it filters and never multiplies rows. A condition that does not translate RAISES: a restriction cannot fall back to memory. Assign the answer back to Source.
entries.parameters: predicate — a function of one row of the source that answers a boolean.

entries.signature: Source.Join(inner, on : Function) | Source.Join(inner, leftKey : Function, rightKey : Function, op : string = "=") : QueryDecorator
entries.description:
Lets a row of the restricted query through only when a permitting row EXISTS in `inner` — a semi-join: it filters, it never multiplies rows. `inner` is a data source (`Data.InformationRegisters.Access`, with its own Where carried along) or a value table.

Two forms: one `on` comparison of a source key with an inner key, `Function(s, a) { return s.Warehouse = a.Warehouse; }`; or two key selectors and the comparison as a string — "=", "<>" (or "!="), "<", "<=", ">", ">="; any other string is read as "=". Each key must be ONE column — for a key reached through a reference, restrict with Where instead.

A single-source inner runs as an EXISTS inside the one statement; a value table, or an inner that joins sources of its own, is put into a temporary table first. Where the database has no temporary tables, such an inner is joined as an ordinary join, which may repeat rows.
entries.syntax_block:
Source = Source.Join(Inner, Function(s, a) { return s.<Key> = a.<Key>; });
Source = Source.Join(Inner, Function(s) { return s.<Key>; }, Function(a) { return a.<Key>; }, "=");
entries.syntax_block_ves:
Source = Source.Join(Inner, Function(s, a) Return s.<Key> = a.<Key>; EndFunction);
Source = Source.Join(Inner, Function(s) Return s.<Key>; EndFunction, Function(a) Return a.<Key>; EndFunction, "=");
entries.parameters:
inner — a Queryable (Data.<Kind>.<Name>, optionally with its own Where) or a value Table.
on — a function of (sourceRow, innerRow) comparing one key of each.
leftKey, rightKey — functions naming one key column on each side.
op — the comparison, as a string; left out, "=".
entries.example:
Allowed = Data.InformationRegisters.WarehouseAccess.Where(Function(a) { return a.User = SessionParameters.User; });
Source = Source.Join(Allowed, Function(s, a) { return s.Warehouse = a.Warehouse; });
